newsitem.title: USA: U.S. won't stand idly by in Iraq - top officer.
newsitem.headline: U.S. won't stand idly by in Iraq - top officer.

text.p: The United States will not stand by idly if Iraqi President Saddam Hussein harms his ethnic minorities or threatens regional stability, the top U.S. uniformed officer said on Sunday.

But in a television interview, General John Shalikashvili, chairman of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff, appeared to play down the Iraqi role in fresh fighting involving rival Kurdish factions in the safe haven set up by the West in northern Iraq after the 1991 Gulf War.
Shalikashvili spoke on the NBC News program "Meet the Press" after a spokesman for one of the Kurdish factions said its rival, backed by Iraqi forces, had captured the towns of Degala and Koi Sanjak.

Iraqi-backed forces of the Kurdistan Democratic Party appeared to be trying to wrest territory from the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan, which reported the fall of the two towns on Sunday, he said. Shalikashvili said Saddam had withdrawn all but "hundreds" of his troops from the northern safe haven after the United States fired 44 cruise missiles into southern Iraq because of his drive in support of the KDP last week.

"I don't know to what degree there's active assistance" by Saddam in the latest KDP offensive, Shalikashvili said. "But what you're seeing is Kurdish fighting .... The United States, rather than siding with one Kurdish faction, against another, which I believe would have been wrong, has always put its effort on trying to get the two sides together to resolve their differences so peace can once again return to the Kurdish area."

But, Shalikashvili said, the United States will not stand "idly by" if Saddam threatens his people or the region. Pressed on whether the United might intervene to confront Saddam in the north, Shalikashvili said Washington had always been very careful not to signal Saddam what it would do.
